doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Not reading music: Wes Montgomery, Dizzy and Japan
summary: Brown notes Wes Montgomery could not read, and recalls Dizzy Gillespie telling her 'If you can hear it, you can sing it' before the Budokan, though she reads no music herself.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: But he had a good ear though.

A great ear. And I think that that’s — Dizzy Gillespie told me that once when I got a chance to go to Japan the very first time. I went to Japan with Dizzy Gillespie and the Modern Jazz Quartet, and Sonny Stitt. And I was just so apprehensive because we were going to play the Budokan, and here I was this rhythm & blues artist, you know. And Dizzy said, “If you can hear it, you can sing it.” And I could always hear it. I don’t read

either, don’t read a note, you know, but always there are a lot of pictures of me looking at the music. It looks good. It gives me status, you know. Especially when I went to go into the studios with the likes of your Arnett Cobbs and your Count Basies and your Billy Eckstines, and I got to be on tour with these great people. Whenever there was an opportunity to pose with them, there is always a piece of music, you know. It may look as though I knew, but no, that’s, it’s really not necessary, especially like the music I’m proud to be a part of, it came from inside.
